meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: Wanting more than you were given
Joy borrowed from other people's harvest

world_behind.title: This follows a body count
world_behind.text: Alma 28 ended by calling for laborers in the vineyard and totaling fifteen years of dead. Alma 29 opens with a man wishing he could reach everyone at once.

world_behind.title: Alma had been visited by an angel
world_behind.text: Mosiah 27 gives the account: a voice like thunder, and Alma struck down. The wish in verse 1 is for the office he once had aimed at him.

world_behind.title: He rebukes himself in the third verse
world_behind.text: No prophet corrects him and no revelation interrupts. Alma states the wish, calls it sin, and works out why over the next five verses. 2 Nephi 4:17 to 19 is the only comparable passage in the volume, where Nephi opens his own soul the same way without any external rebuke.

world_behind.title: The chapter runs on the word desire
world_behind.text: Verses 4 and 5 have God grant each man according to his desire, whether that ends in life or in death. Alma 41:5 states the same rule to Corianton twelve chapters later, as the mechanism of the restoration. Alma applies it to his own wish first.

world_behind.title: He knows about other nations' teachers
world_behind.text: Verse 8 says the Lord grants every nation, in their own tongue, to teach his word. 2 Nephi 29:12 says the same thing from the other side, that he speaks to the Jews, the Nephites and the other tribes and each writes it. The doctrine that the record is one of several is stated in both halves of the volume.

world_behind.title: The captivity is his family's memory
world_behind.text: Verses 11 and 12 recall the deliverance from bondage under Amulon, and Alma reaches past it to Egypt. His father's escape from Helam is joined to the exodus.

world_behind.title: The sons of Mosiah have just come home
world_behind.text: Verse 14 makes their success the reason his joy is fuller than his own success would make it. Alma 27 recorded the meeting; this is what he did with it afterward.

words.text: Treated at Mosiah 26:25, where the Lord names the second trump. Alma's use here is a wish: he wants a voice that carries like the instrument, and the King James Bible attaches the same word to the resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15 and 1 Thessalonians 4.

Assigned as a portion, the way land is divided. The word occurs once in scripture, and its verb form allotteth occurs once, in the next verse. Alma says he ought to be content with what the Lord has allotted him, which puts his calling in the category of an inheritance.

Not to be changed. The record uses it twice, both in Alma; the other is Alma 41, where the decrees of God are unalterable and the way is open to whoever will walk in it. Here the fixed thing is God granting men according to their desires.

Not chargeable with fault. The record uses it seven times and the King James Bible fifteen. Alma applies it to the person who cannot tell good from evil, which makes knowledge the thing that creates exposure.

Biting regret. It appears three times in the record, and never in the King James Bible, always in Alma, and always paired with conscience. It is the last item in his list of what a man may be granted according to his desires.

Being held as a prisoner or a subject people. The record uses the word sixty-one times. Alma names it twice here, of his own fathers under Amulon, and then folds it into the Egyptian bondage, so that one family's escape and a nation's are told as the same act by the same God.

phrases.term: O that I were an angel, and could have the wish of mine heart
phrases.text: The most quoted line Alma wrote, and the chapter spends fifteen verses walking it back. He wants a trump, a voice to shake the earth, and repentance cried to every people.

phrases.term: I am a man, and do sin in my wish
phrases.text: Alma names his own error in seven words. The wish was for more reach in a good cause, and he calls wanting it a sin because it argues with what he was given.

phrases.term: I ought to be content with the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me
phrases.text: The correction, stated as a duty rather than a feeling. Paul told the Philippians he had learned contentment in whatever state he was in (Philip. 4:11); Alma says he ought to have it and admits he does not.

phrases.term: He granteth unto men according to their desire, whether it be unto death or unto life
phrases.text: The doctrine Alma uses on himself. God gives people what they want, in both directions, and the decrees behind that are unalterable. His wish for a louder voice runs against a system that is already working.

phrases.term: He that knoweth not good from evil is blameless
phrases.text: A one-line statement about accountability. Ignorance clears a man; knowledge puts him under the same rule Alma has just described. Alma 42 and 2 Nephi 2 build the same point at length.

phrases.term: Why should I desire more than to perform the work to which I have been called?
phrases.text: The turn of the chapter. Having established the doctrine, Alma applies it as a question about his own ambition, and the next two verses give his answer.

phrases.term: The Lord doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word
phrases.text: Alma's reason for standing down. Other peoples have their own teachers, in their own languages, receiving what God sees fit for them to have. The wish to reach every people was unnecessary because the work is already distributed.

phrases.term: I do not glory of myself, but I glory in that which the Lord hath commanded me
phrases.text: Alma makes the same distinction Ammon made to Aaron in Alma 26. Both men accept the word for boasting and relocate the subject of it, and both land on being an instrument.

phrases.term: That same God who delivered them out of the hands of the Egyptians
phrases.text: Alma joins his father's escape from Amulon to the exodus in one sentence. The point of the repetition of "that same God" is that the deliverance from Helam was not a lesser kind of event.

phrases.term: My joy is more full because of the success of my brethren
phrases.text: Alma says other men's results please him more than his own. He has just been given much success by his own account in verse 13, and he ranks the mission to the Lamanites above it.

phrases.term: Even to the separation of it from the body, as it were
phrases.text: Alma describes joy at somebody else's harvest almost taking him out of himself. Ammon went to the ground for the same reason in Alma 27, and Alma stayed standing then and reports the sensation now.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The famous verse is withdrawn two verses later
verses.text: "O that I were an angel... and cry repentance unto every people" is the line the chapter is remembered for, and verse 3 takes it back: "But behold, I am a man, and do sin in my wish; for I ought to be content with the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me." The record prints the wish at full stretch, then prints the retraction, and keeps both. What follows is not a sermon on desire but Alma reasoning himself out of one.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: The chapter's whole moral vocabulary sits in one verse
verses.text: Good and evil appear four times each in verse 5 and nowhere else in the chapter: "he that knoweth not good from evil is blameless; but he that knoweth good and evil, to him it is given according to his desires." The pairs are stacked, desire against desire, life against death, joy against remorse. Everything the other sixteen verses lean on is set down here and nowhere else.

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: Two questions, and the answer is about other people
verses.text: The only questions in the chapter are consecutive, and the second quotes the first verse back as an interrogative: "Why should I desire that I were an angel, that I could speak unto all the ends of the earth?" Verse 8 answers with something outside Alma entirely: "the Lord doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word." He does not need a voice to shake the earth because other nations already have teachers.

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: One word, turned over four times
verses.text: Glory is used four times in verse 9 and never again in the chapter: "I glory in it. I do not glory of myself, but I glory in that which the Lord hath commanded me; yea, and this is my glory." The word is turned over until it changes hands, and what it finally settles on is not an achievement but a possibility, "that perhaps I may be an instrument."

verses.label: v. 11–13
verses.title: One phrase carries the argument from Egypt to Alma
verses.text: "That same God" stands at the head of verses 12 and 13, and scripture has the phrase in only three other places; Limhi puts it to the same work at Mosiah 7:20. It binds three things in one movement: the God who delivered the fathers from the Egyptians, the God who established the church among them, and the God who "hath called me by a holy calling." Alma argues his authority by identity and not by office.

verses.label: v. 14–16
verses.title: The joy is handed to someone else
verses.text: "I do not joy in my own success alone, but my joy is more full because of the success of my brethren." Success is confined to verses 13 through 16, and it crosses from Alma's to theirs inside that span. The chapter that opened wanting one voice for the whole earth closes on the labors of the men who went up to the land of Nephi without him.

chapter.title: The famous line is the thing being corrected
chapter.text: Verse 1 is quoted far more often than verse 3, and Alma wrote them together. The chapter is a man taking back a wish in public.

chapter.title: Ambition in a good cause is still called sin
chapter.text: Verses 1 and 2 state the wish, to be an angel with a trump crying repentance. Verse 3 retracts it and names the fault, "I am a man, and do sin in my wish; for I ought to be content with the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me." Verse 4 gives the reason and it is about God's arrangement rather than about pride, "I ought not to harrow up in my desires the firm decree of a just God." Verses 6 and 7 then restate the retraction as two questions. A desire for wider preaching is classified as sin in the same paragraph that expresses it.

chapter.title: His argument against himself is theological
chapter.text: He does not say the wish is impractical. He says God grants men according to their desires, that the decrees are unalterable, and that arguing with them is out of order.

chapter.title: The world is already staffed
chapter.text: Verse 8 says every nation gets teachers in its own tongue, receiving what God sees fit. That single verse dissolves the need for the angel, and it is the chapter's largest claim.

chapter.title: Contentment is stated as an obligation
chapter.text: I ought to be content. Alma treats it as owed rather than felt, which lets him admit he is not there while still knowing what is required.

chapter.title: Memory is his engine
chapter.text: Seeing the penitent makes him remember his own conversion; that makes him remember the captivity; that makes him remember Egypt. Three rememberings stack into the reason he keeps working.

chapter.title: He ranks other men's results above his own
chapter.text: Verse 14 says his joy is fuller for the mission he did not go on. The chapter that began with wanting a bigger voice ends with rejoicing over somebody else's harvest.

chapter.title: The last word is a prayer for other people's converts
chapter.text: Verse 17 asks that the sons of Mosiah and all the fruit of their labors be seated and go no more out. Alma closes his own soliloquy by naming somebody else's list.

applications.title: Say the wish, then examine it
applications.text: Alma wrote the wish down in full, an angel's trump and a voice to shake the earth, and then examined it in the next verse. Getting a desire onto the page is what makes it possible to look at, and he does both in public.

applications.title: Take your assignment as an allotment
applications.text: He names the fault precisely, "I ought to be content with the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me." Discontent with your portion is treated here as a claim about somebody else's judgment rather than as an appetite.

applications.title: Ask whether the wish disputes a decree
applications.text: The test he applies is not whether the desire is noble but whether it "harrow[s] up in my desires the firm decree of a just God." A good thing wanted in the wrong place is still out of place.

applications.title: Ask why you would need more than your calling
applications.text: The question he puts to himself is plain, "why should I desire more than to perform the work to which I have been called?" Put it to yourself about the enlargement you have been wishing for.

applications.title: Remember that other people have teachers too
applications.text: Alma stands down on the ground that "the Lord doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word." The reach you were wishing for is already covered by somebody else's assignment.

applications.title: Glory in the commandment rather than in yourself
applications.text: He draws the line exactly, "I do not glory of myself, but I glory in that which the Lord hath commanded me." The distinction is available in almost any account you give of your own work.

applications.title: Let the memory do the work
applications.text: When he sees people repent, "then do I remember what the Lord has done for me." His own history is what supplies the joy in somebody else's turning, which means the two are connected rather than competing.

applications.title: Rejoice at the harvest you had no part in
applications.text: Alma's fullest joy is over other men's results, "I do not joy in my own success alone, but my joy is more full because of the success of my brethren." He then asks that they, and everyone converted by them, be brought in.

questions.text: What do I wish I were, and what would I do with it?
Is there a good thing I want that would mean God gave me the wrong assignment?
If God grants people according to their desires, what am I actually desiring?
What is the work I have been called to, said plainly?
Whose prayer was answered when I changed?
What deliverance in my family's history do I still tell?
Whose success have I found it hard to enjoy?
